name: On-Chain vs Off-Chain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What Actually Lives on the Ledger: On-Chain vs Off-Chain
lesson.summary: On-chain refers to data and activity recorded directly on a blockchain and subject to its consensus rules, while off-chain refers to activity that happens elsewhere and is only reconciled with the chain occasionally, and this distinction is the foundation of nearly every blockchain scaling technique.
lesson.body:
A blockchain, as defined earlier, is a ledger that every full node independently stores and verifies. On-chain simply means anything written into that ledger and processed according to the network's own consensus rules and ordering, a Bitcoin transfer, an Ethereum smart contract call, a token mint. Off-chain means the opposite: any activity, agreement, or record keeping that happens outside that consensus process entirely, whether it is two people privately exchanging signed messages, a company's internal database, or a centralized exchange's own order book.

The reason this distinction matters so much comes directly from the scalability trilemma covered earlier. Every on-chain action has to be independently processed, validated, and permanently stored by a broad, decentralized set of nodes, which is precisely the resource intensive property that caps a blockchain's throughput in the first place. Moving activity off-chain lets participants transact freely, and cheaply, without asking the entire network to process every step, and then only settle a final, aggregated result back on-chain once. This single idea, do the work off-chain, settle the result on-chain, is the shared foundation underneath essentially every layer 2 scaling technique covered later in this section, including state channels and sidechains.

A concrete, already familiar example is a centralized cryptocurrency exchange. When a user buys and sells an asset repeatedly on such an exchange, none of those individual trades touch the blockchain at all, they are simply updates to the exchange's own internal ledger, which can handle far more trades per second than any blockchain because it is not decentralized. Only the user's initial deposit into the exchange, and their eventual withdrawal back out, are actual on-chain transactions. This is exactly why an exchange can advertise trading speeds far beyond what the underlying blockchain itself supports.

That efficiency comes at a real cost, though, and it is not a free lunch. On-chain activity is independently verified by the network's own consensus mechanism, which is the source of a blockchain's core trust guarantee, nobody has to take any single party's word for it. Off-chain activity has no such independent verification built in, so moving a transaction off-chain necessarily means trusting whatever party is keeping the off-chain record, the exchange, the channel counterparty, the sidechain operator, to behave honestly, at least until the moment activity is finally settled back on-chain.

Recognizing this trade off, throughput and cost savings in exchange for reintroduced trust in some off-chain party, is the right lens for evaluating the specific scaling designs covered next. Layer 1 describes the base chain itself, and layer 2 solutions, state channels, and sidechains each represent a different, specific way of drawing the line between what stays on-chain and what moves off.
